chunks: Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In

a man who accused his wife of adultery while she was in one of the villages, and the ruler/sultan said, 'I have no knowledge of this; you are in Kufa.' So she came to the judge to perform *li'an* (mutual imprecation), but she died before they performed *li'an*. They said to the husband, 'These [other heirs] have no inheritance for you [i.e., you get the whole estate or the specific share? No, the context implies the husband's share is affected or the other heirs are excluded].' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If a man from her family stands in her place and performs *li'an* with her, he has no inheritance. And if one of her guardians refuses to stand in her place, the husband takes the inheritance.'
ai.seo_question: What happens to inheritance if a wife dies before li'an is completed and a relative performs it on her behalf?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses the procedural nuance of *li'an* when the wife dies before the judicial imprecation is finalized, highlighting the role of her male guardian (*wali*) in standing in her stead. It establishes that if a relative performs *li'an* on her behalf, he is excluded from inheritance to prevent conflict of interest, whereas if no one acts, the husband retains his share, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on the guardian's active participation in completing the evidentiary process.
